headline: Yu Liu and twenty-one co-authors halved the DRAM bit cell to 2F² by bonding a wafer face-down and building a second cell on its backside, and report 27.5 percent less parasitic load, 11 percent more sense margin and half the area against a 4F² baseline.

items.title: Two DRAM cells back to back across a bond, and the bitline gets quieter
items.dek: Yu Liu and twenty-one co-authors report the first Flip DRAM: a wafer bonded face-down and thinned from the back so a second one-transistor, one-capacitor bit cell can be built on the far side, cutting cell area from four to two squared minimum feature sizes.
items.why_it_matters: Sense margin in a one-transistor, one-capacitor DRAM is set by charge sharing — the cell dumps its charge onto a bitline carrying far more capacitance than the cell has, so the sense amplifier sees only the fraction set by that ratio. Cutting reported parasitics by 27.5 percent at the same mat size is what buys the 11 percent better sense margin and 16.3 percent faster charge sharing, and that is headroom the storage capacitor has been giving back for a decade as its hole gets deeper and narrower.
items.background_md: A DRAM bit is one transistor and one capacitor, and the design is a fight over a capacitance ratio. The capacitor must hold enough charge to be read, but it sits in a hole tens of nanometres wide and about a micrometre deep — aspect ratios near 100:1 for roughly 6–7 fF. When the access transistor opens, that charge spreads onto a bitline with several times more capacitance, so the sense amplifier sees a small fraction of what was stored. Cell area is quoted in F², the squared minimum printable feature: 8F² gave way to 6F², and 4F² is the current target.
items.deeper_md:
4F² is already the hard target, and it needs a vertical channel transistor — source under channel under drain — because a planar access device cannot keep its channel length inside a 2F × 2F tile. The Flip route does not shrink that transistor further. It bonds the processed wafer face-down, thins the substrate away, and builds a second self-aligned vertical channel on the exposed backside, so two 1T1C cells sit back to back and the pair occupies the footprint one used to.

The process modules the authors say they developed are the self-aligned stacked vertical channel, bitline and word-line formation, wafer bonding and flipping, substrate thinning, and a low-resistance cobalt storage node, chosen against thermal, misalignment and parasitic risk. Against 4F² VCT at the same mat size their device-to-chip DTCO framework gives 27.5 percent less parasitics, 11 percent better sense margin, 16.3 percent faster charge sharing and 50 percent less area. A 3D-DRAM variant that flips the word-line staircase instead reports 25 percent density gain, 15.1 percent faster turn-on and 6.8 percent less charge-sharing time.

What is absent: a working array, a retention distribution, a yield figure. Process modules plus a model are not a part, and the preprint is two days old with nobody on the outside having checked it.

glossary.definition: Cell footprint expressed in squared minimum printable features, so it compares layouts independently of node: a 4F² cell occupies a 2F × 2F tile, one bitline pitch by one word-line pitch.
The standard DRAM bit cell — one access transistor gating one storage capacitor — which loses its charge to leakage and therefore has to be read and rewritten periodically.

The read step: opening the access transistor connects the cell capacitor to the bitline, and the two redistribute charge, so the voltage swing the amplifier gets is set by the ratio of the two capacitances.

An access device with source, channel and drain stacked along the surface normal rather than laid out side by side, which keeps channel length while shrinking the footprint to about one squared feature.

items.title: CFET loses on every cell metric and wins once the chip is routed
items.dek: Hussam Amrouch's group at the Technical University of Munich, with Applied Materials, ran identical device models through a layout-to-TCAD parasitic flow and found that stacking the n- and p-transistor vertically — a complementary FET — costs 6.1 percent in standard-cell delay but cuts an AI accelerator's area by 24.7 percent.
items.why_it_matters: The cell gets slower and the chip gets faster, and the reason is wiring: a denser cell shortens the metal between cells, 12 percent of total wirelength in this design, and wire delay is most of what the faster cell was paying for. That inverts the usual way a device option is screened. A team judging complementary FETs on extracted cell timing alone would have read every number in this study as a reason not to build one.
items.background_md: A standard cell's speed is not set only by its transistors. Most of the capacitance a gate has to drive is parasitic — the contacts, the local metal levels, and the coupling between them — and that fraction grows as pitches shrink, because the conductors get closer together faster than they get smaller. Putting the p-type device directly above the n-type one removes the n-to-p spacing from the cell width, but it also stacks their contacts and routes signal and power past two device tiers instead of one. Whether the trade pays only exists as a number after a layout has been extracted with a field solver.
items.deeper_md:
The two technologies compared are an A10 nanosheet node at 46 nm contacted poly pitch, 4-track cell height and 20 nm M0 pitch, and an A7 CFET at 44 nm CPP, 3.5 tracks and 18 nm M0, with the same calibrated device model used for both so that only the parasitics differ. Layouts go to 3D TCAD automatically and the RC comes out of a field solver.

At the cell, CFET is worse on everything: input pin capacitance 9.7 percent higher, cell delay 6.1 percent longer, transition time 5.0 percent longer, internal power 3.4 percent higher, against 24.3 percent average area reduction. Implemented as a 32 × 32 multiply-accumulate systolic array at matched 61.7 percent utilisation, the chip goes from 17,296 µm² to 13,017 µm², wirelength falls 12 percent, and area efficiency rises 74 percent in TOPS/mm². Run at iso-frequency, CFET needs 0.56 V where nanosheet needs 1.0 V: power density 55 W/cm² against 148, junction temperature 62 °C against 125, and because bias-temperature instability is exponential in temperature, ten-year ΔV_th falls from 61 mV to 37 mV and the aging guardband by 53 percent.

The caveat is that chain. Every number after the temperature inherits the thermal model, and the same group's earlier work puts self-heating in a two-tier CFET at 62–74 K above ambient. One benchmark design, and a tool vendor among the authors.

glossary.definition: Centre-to-centre distance between adjacent gates, which fixes how much room a cell has for contacts and local wiring and is the number that stops shrinking first.
Cell height counted in routing-metal pitches; a 3.5-track cell is 3.5 M0 pitches tall, so it sets density more directly than the marketing node name does.
Slow threshold-voltage drift caused by charge trapping at the gate dielectric under bias, accelerating sharply with temperature, which is why designers reserve timing margin for a chip's tenth year.
Trillions of operations per second divided by silicon area — the density figure a fixed-function accelerator is judged on, since it combines how fast the array runs with how much room it took.

items.fab_angle: The lesson for anyone choosing a library is that an extracted cell timing table is the wrong place to judge a stacked-device option: the penalty is visible there and the payoff only appears after place-and-route.

items.title: Flip half the crystal over and the high overtones stop cancelling themselves
items.dek: A group led by Ruochen Lu bonded two 40-micrometre lithium niobate plates with opposite polarisation into one 80-micrometre stack, and it drives thickness-shear acoustic overtones out to 1.75 gigahertz — modes a single plate barely excites, because the charge they generate cancels against itself.
items.why_it_matters: An acoustic resonator is judged on frequency multiplied by quality factor, and the two normally fight, because raising frequency on a single plate means thinning the plate and paying for it in surface and anchor loss. Running a thick plate on its 26th overtone raises frequency while keeping the bulk: 11,338 quality factor at 0.77 gigahertz at room temperature, an fQ product of 8.74 × 10¹². What it costs is coupling, which falls from 39.6 percent on the second mode to 0.04 percent on the 46th.
items.background_md: A piezoelectric plate between two electrodes rings at a frequency set by its thickness, and also at overtones of that fundamental. Overtones are attractive because the plate stays thick — thickness is what sets anchor and surface loss, so a thick plate keeps a high quality factor — while the frequency climbs with mode number. The obstacle is electrical rather than mechanical. In a high-order mode the strain reverses sign several times through the thickness, so the charge those regions push onto a single pair of electrodes largely cancels, and the coupling available to drive or read the mode collapses toward nothing.
items.deeper_md:
The stack is two 40 µm X-cut lithium niobate layers direct-bonded with their polar axes opposed, sitting on silicon through a silicon-dioxide interlayer, with a patterned top electrode, a floating bottom electrode and an air cavity opened by a deep silicon etch. Reversing polarity halfway through the thickness lines the charge up with the strain reversal instead of against it, which is why coupling survives at all at high order.

The measured ladder, at 12 K, runs: 2nd mode 46.41 MHz, k² 39.60 percent, Q 712; 6th 176.29 MHz, 3.87 percent, 3,771; 10th 297.91 MHz, 0.88 percent, 14,019; 26th 779.27 MHz, 0.13 percent, 20,507; 30th 899.39 MHz, 0.10 percent, 19,273; 46th 1,379.55 MHz, 0.04 percent, 14,333. At room temperature the same device gives Q of 11,338 and 11,917 at 0.77 and 0.89 GHz, for fQ of 8.74 × 10¹² and 1.06 × 10¹³ Hz; the cryogenic peak fQ is 1.98 × 10¹³ Hz.

Two things the authors flag themselves. Measured k² sits systematically below simulation, which they put down to fabrication non-idealities. And Q stops improving as temperature falls further, which says surface, interface and anchor damping dominate at that point rather than intrinsic material loss — so the cryogenic numbers are a statement about the mount, not about lithium niobate.

glossary.definition: The fraction of energy a piezoelectric device converts between electrical and mechanical form per cycle; it sets how wide a filter built from the resonator can be, so a small k² is a hard limit, not an inefficiency.
Energy stored divided by energy lost per radian of oscillation; a resonance of Q = 10,000 has a fractional bandwidth of one part in ten thousand and rings for roughly that many cycles.
Frequency times quality factor, used as the figure of merit because most loss mechanisms make Q fall as frequency rises, so their product is roughly a material and mount constant.

A bulk vibration in which layers of the plate slide sideways past each other rather than compressing, with the displacement varying through the thickness — the mode a quartz crystal oscillator also uses.

items.fab_angle: The whole structure is cleanroom-recognisable: a direct bond through a silicon-dioxide interlayer, a deep silicon etch to release the membrane, and a bottom electrode that is never contacted. The hard step is the bond itself, because the trick depends on the two plates meeting with their polar axes exactly opposed.

items.title: Two memories: one for the regular half of a graph, one for the ragged half
items.dek: A team presenting at the ESSERC 2026 solid-state circuits conference has measured ETHEREAL, a 28-nanometre chip running graph neural networks over event-camera data — cameras whose pixels report brightness changes independently instead of sending frames — at 25.6 microseconds and 1.7 microjoules per event at 640 × 480.
items.why_it_matters: Event data has been fed to ordinary frame networks largely because its sparse half wrecks a normal memory hierarchy: every new event needs its neighbours in space and time, and those addresses are not known until the event arrives. Splitting the memory in two — a sixteen-bank interleaved array for the neighbours that are adjacent by construction, and an eight-way set-associative cache keyed on most-recent timestamp for the ones that are not — is what moves this from the 5.1 milliseconds an FPGA implementation needed down to tens of microseconds, at four times the input resolution.
items.background_md: A conventional image sensor reports every pixel on a clock whether or not anything changed. A dynamic vision sensor does the opposite: each pixel independently emits an event — a coordinate, a timestamp and a sign — when its own brightness crosses a threshold, at microsecond resolution and with no frames at all. That output is a sparse set of points in space and time, and the natural way to process it is as a graph whose nodes are events and whose edges join events close in both. The difficulty is that graph work mixes dense arithmetic with memory accesses whose addresses only exist at runtime.
items.deeper_md:
The chip is TSMC 28 nm, 3.7 mm², 0.6–1 V, clocked up to 250 MHz, with 1.25 MB of SRAM divided into a 3D cache, a 3D buffer and a 2D scratchpad. Its convolution engine evaluates B-spline kernels, which is the trick that makes compute cost independent of kernel size because each basis function has local support — the same idea as SplineCNN, moved into hardware and run over several neighbours in parallel.

The memory split is the contribution. Node data that is adjacent in the image plane goes to a 16-bank 2D-interleaved memory so several neighbours stream at once, reported as a 3.8× latency improvement. The irregular part — neighbours in the time dimension — goes to an 8-way set-associative cache that tracks the most recent timestamp per region, reaching a 58 percent hit rate and 2.4× fewer external memory reads. Across workloads the measured spread is 17.8–36.5 µs and 1.1–2.3 µJ per inference.

Caveats: the accuracy figures are end-to-end simulated rather than read off the die, the GPU comparison is against an A100 built for a different design point, and 28 nm means the energy number would look better on a modern node rather than worse — which cuts in the authors' favour and should be said as such.

glossary.definition: One pixel's report that its log brightness crossed a threshold, carrying x, y, a microsecond timestamp and a polarity bit — and nothing about the pixels that did not change.

A convolution whose kernel is a continuous B-spline evaluated at each neighbour's relative position, so it works on irregular point sets and costs the same regardless of how large the neighbourhood radius is.
A cache that lets any address land in one of N slots within its set; eight-way means eight candidate lines per set, trading comparator hardware for a lower chance of evicting something still wanted.
Splitting one memory into independently addressed arrays so several reads proceed in the same cycle; interleaving addresses across banks is what makes spatially adjacent data land in different banks.

items.title: Move the weights to flash and DRAM stops needing HBM's bandwidth per byte
items.dek: Pengfei Xia and co-authors modelled a one-node appliance that keeps a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model's weights in High Bandwidth Flash — stacked NAND standardised through the Open Compute Project in August — and found the DRAM left behind needs 8 to 24 times less bandwidth per byte than HBM3e.
items.why_it_matters: Bandwidth per byte, not bandwidth, is what forces a machine onto high-bandwidth memory: HBM3e can read its whole capacity about 33 times a second, and that ratio exists because dense decoding touches every weight for every token. Move the weights to flash and the DRAM tier is holding key-value state, which is re-read far less often, so 1.4 to 4.0 reads per second suffices — a ratio ordinary LPDDR modules already meet. The same argument then caps what the flash has to expose to the host rather than hold internally.
items.background_md: Memory for an accelerator is usually specified with two numbers quoted apart: how many bytes it holds, and how many bytes per second it moves. What actually constrains a serving machine is their ratio — how many times per second the whole tier can be read end to end. Dense transformer decoding reads every weight for every token, so that ratio has to be high, and high-bandwidth memory stacked beside the die is the expensive answer. Mixture-of-experts models break the assumption underneath it: only a small share of the parameters is touched per token, so most of the capacity sits untouched between reads.
items.deeper_md:
The specification behind this is real and recent: Sandisk and SK hynix disclosed HBF through the Open Compute Project on 4 August 2026 — up to 512 GB per package from 8-high and 16-high NAND stacks, three bandwidth grades spanning roughly 0.4 to 3.0 TB/s, with UCIe as the host interface.

The model fixes a 450 TFLOP/s FP8 compute die and two MoE configurations: 1.6 T parameters with 49 B active, 384 routed experts at top-6, 865 GB quantised; and 2.8 T with 104 B active, 896 experts at top-16, 1,560 GB. Holding completion time within 1.10× of an unconstrained reference and a 256 GB floor on the state tier, required state bandwidth-to-capacity comes out at 4.0 s⁻¹ and 1.4 s⁻¹ against HBM3e's 33.3 s⁻¹, and eight LPCAMM2 modules (512 GB, 1.09 TB/s) clear both. On the flash side, six packages exposing 384 GB/s each give 2.30 TB/s aggregate — 62.5 percent below the 6.14 TB/s the packages hold internally, an exposure ratio of 0.24.

This is a provisioning study, not a machine. HBF internal parallelism is idealised, the workloads are three synthetic multi-turn agentic traces, expert occupancy comes from a Pólya-urn calibration rather than trace replay, speculative decoding is pinned at 4.27 accepted tokens, and packaging parasitics and real integration are out of scope.

glossary.definition: A model whose feed-forward layers are split into many expert sub-networks, of which a router selects a handful per token, so parameter count grows without the arithmetic per token growing with it.
Bytes per second divided by bytes held — how many times a second the tier can be read end to end. HBM3e sits near 33 s⁻¹; a DDR DIMM is one to two orders of magnitude below that.
Stacked NAND packaged like HBM and read over a wide die-to-die link, aimed at read-mostly data such as model weights; capacity per package is far larger than DRAM's and latency far worse.

The cached keys and values from every token already processed, which an attention layer re-reads to generate the next token; it grows with context length and is the part of inference memory that changes constantly.

items.title: The lease protocol was safe; the timer that started it was not
items.dek: Márton Trencséni went back to PaxosLease, the disk-free lease algorithm he published in 2012, built a machine-checked model of it in TLA+, and found that starting the lease timer when the proposer's prepare quorum arrives lets two nodes hold the same exclusive lease at once.
items.why_it_matters: A lease is how a distributed system grants exclusive rights without a shared clock, and its entire safety argument is an argument about elapsed time. The model puts a number on the piece that was previously left informal: after a node granting leases loses its in-memory state, it must refuse to take part for at least the full duration of one acquisition attempt, and that bound is checked tight in both directions. It also finds a second way to get two owners that no quarantine length fixes.
items.background_md: A lease is a lock with an expiry. One node holds exclusive rights to something — being the leader, owning a shard — for a fixed interval, and if it dies, the others wait out the clock rather than trying to detect the failure. Making that safe without synchronised clocks means reasoning in elapsed time on each node instead of wall time, under arbitrary message delay and reordering. Implementations also want to keep disk writes off the acquisition path, which means the nodes granting a lease hold their state only in memory, and therefore forget everything the moment they restart.
items.deeper_md:
Three results. First, the restart quarantine a lease acceptor owes after losing volatile state equals the proposer's attempt duration; TLC confirms the bound is tight in both directions and TLAPS discharges the timing arithmetic. Second, timer placement is a safety property, not a tuning knob: starting the attempt timer on receipt of the prepare quorum — rather than at the start of the attempt — admits two concurrent owners, which makes the 2012 paper's rule unsafe as written. Third, when a proposer abandons an attempt and retries, leftover messages from the abandoned attempt can make acceptors report a lease the proposer appears to own; unless such reports count only while that specific lease is being actively renewed, two owners are reachable no matter how long the quarantine is.

The artifact is worth as much as the paper. It carries the TLA+ specs and TLC configurations, deliberately weakened variants for which TLC produces a two-owner trace, a TLAPS support-obligation module, and a separate executable Python reference model encoding the same rules independently.

The limit is that this is a model. The bound holds against the paper's timing abstraction, and the two encodings share an author, so their agreement is weaker evidence than two independent teams would be.

glossary.definition: In Paxos-family protocols, a node that votes on proposals; safety comes from the fact that any two quorums of acceptors overlap, so a later quorum always contains someone who saw the earlier decision.
Any set of nodes large enough that two such sets must share a member — normally a majority — which is what makes it impossible for two conflicting decisions to both be accepted.
A specification language for concurrent systems and its model checker, which explores every reachable interleaving of a finite instance and prints a counterexample trace when an invariant breaks.
The interval a restarted node must sit out before answering protocol messages again, because it has forgotten the promises it made and could otherwise vote twice on the same round.

items.title: A lossless decoder is lossless in FP32 and something else in BF16
items.dek: Ilya Koziev, Leonid Sinev and Ivan Oseledets re-ran Orthrus — a decoder claiming to emit exactly the tokens its autoregressive backbone would, while generating several at a time — and reproduced the reference sequence on 45 percent of 1,190 prompts in bfloat16, and on all of them in float32.
items.why_it_matters: Losslessness is a property of an algorithm that only holds on hardware if the arithmetic cooperates: the acceptance test compares quantities computed down two different code paths, and with eight mantissa bits those paths disagree often enough to flip an argmax. One flipped token puts generation on a different trajectory, so the divergence compounds rather than washing out. The practical consequence is that an exactness claim owes a numerical precision alongside it, and that benchmark scores cannot check it — all three downstream tasks scored the same either way.
items.background_md: Autoregressive generation is serial by construction: the model must see token n before it can compute token n+1, so an accelerator spends most of decoding waiting on memory rather than doing arithmetic. Speculative decoding attacks that by guessing several tokens cheaply and then verifying them in one parallel pass of the expensive model, keeping the longest prefix the verification accepts. The acceptance rule is deliberately designed so the output distribution is provably identical to plain decoding, which is why the technique is considered safe to switch on by default. The proof assumes exact arithmetic.
items.deeper_md:
Orthrus (Nguyen et al., May 2026) bolts a lightweight diffusion view onto a frozen autoregressive model, both views reading the same KV cache; the autoregressive head prefills, the diffusion head emits in parallel, and an exact consensus between the two views is the acceptance test. The claim is up to 7.8× speedup with O(1) cache overhead and lossless output.

The replication covers 1,190 prompts across 12 domains. In BF16, exact trajectory match is 45 percent on the authors' released checkpoint and 43 percent on an independently retrained one, with a domain spread from 11 percent on English poetry to 88 percent on grammatical error correction. Divergence tracks difficulty: response-conditional perplexity averages 1.11 on matching trajectories and 1.28 on diverging ones, with a logistic coefficient of −8.10. Repeating the whole sweep in FP32 gives 100 percent match on all 1,190. Task scores are unmoved either way — GSM8K 0.4238 and 0.4147 against a 0.4003 baseline, HumanEval 0.3659 and 0.4146 against 0.4024, IFEval loose 0.2052 and 0.2181 against 0.2015.

What is not established: which operation causes the divergence, what FP32 costs in throughput, and whether other decoders advertised as lossless behave the same way. The models tested are in the 1.7 B class.

glossary.definition: Producing several candidate tokens with a cheap method, then verifying them in one pass of the expensive model and keeping the accepted prefix; the verification rule is what preserves the original output distribution.

A 16-bit float with the same 8-bit exponent as FP32 but only 7 explicit mantissa bits, so it covers the same dynamic range at roughly three decimal digits of precision — the usual format for model weights and activations.
The exponentiated average negative log-likelihood the model assigns to the response it produced; low values mean the model was confident at every step, which here predicts that two code paths agree.
The stricter test used here: not that two systems score the same, but that they emit the identical token sequence for a prompt, which is the only thing a losslessness claim can mean.

foundations.subtitle: Why the industry stopped printing a whole field at once and started dragging a slit across it — and what that bought in field size, distortion and speed.
foundations.tldr: A projection lens only forms a good image over a limited circle, and dies kept outgrowing it. A scanner sidesteps the problem by illuminating a narrow slit of the best part of the lens and sweeping the mask and the wafer past it in opposite directions, at speeds locked to the reduction ratio. The printed field can then be as long as the stage can travel, and the lens's own distortion gets averaged out along the way — at the price of a new error made entirely of stage motion.

sections.heading: The chip outgrew the lens
sections.body_md:
Start with the thing that does not scale. A projection lens forms a sharp, low-distortion image over a limited circular field, and every aberration gets worse toward its edge. You can buy resolution by raising numerical aperture, and the industry did — from 0.16 on the earliest projection tools to 0.93 on the last dry systems — but a wider *field* at the same quality is a different and much more expensive object, because the glass grows in every dimension at once and each added element brings its own errors.

A stepper prints one rectangular section of the wafer at a time, steps the stage, and prints the next. That works while the die fits inside the lens's good field. Through the 1980s it did. Reduction ratios came down from 10:1 to 5:1 and then 4:1, which shrank mask errors by the same factor and made masks writable. By the early 1990s, though, microprocessors and megabit DRAMs were larger than any affordable lens could image well in one shot, and the choice was a bigger lens or a different way of using the one you had.
sections.deeper_md: Reduction matters more than it looks. At 4× a defect or placement error on the mask lands on the wafer a quarter as large, so mask specification loosens quadratically in area terms; it also means the mask is four times the die in each dimension, which is why a 6-inch mask blank has been the standard for decades and why the reticle stage has to travel four times as far as the wafer stage.

sections.heading: Scanning came first, and lost
sections.body_md:
The odd part of this history is that scanning is the older idea. Perkin-Elmer's Micralign, introduced in 1973, swept a curved slit of light across a mask and a whole wafer together at 1:1 magnification, and it dominated production for most of a decade. It had no reduction, so the mask carried features at full size and every mask defect printed.

Steppers displaced it on yield arithmetic rather than on resolution. A stepper cost well over twice as much per tool, but the defect density attributable to it ran about one per square inch against four for the projection aligners, and because a stepper aligns each field individually rather than accepting one global fit across a warped wafer, overlay improved as well. Cost per *good* die came out around a fifth. The 64 Kbit DRAM generation in 1978 is the marker: several manufacturers could not make the ramp because lithography could not hold the one-micron barrier, and the companies that moved to reduction steppers early are the ones still here.
sections.deeper_md: The overlay argument is worth separating from the defect argument. A 1:1 full-wafer scanner has exactly one chance to fit the mask to the wafer, so wafer distortion from earlier thermal steps shows up as a systematic residue across the whole slice. A stepper re-aligns every field, so it fits a small local model many times instead of one global model once, and the residual scales with field size rather than wafer size.

sections.heading: The compromise: a slit that also steps
sections.body_md:
Step-and-scan, arriving in the early 1990s, takes the useful half of each approach. The illumination is narrowed to a rectangle covering only the best-corrected part of the lens field — Chris Mack's worked example is 25 mm × 8 mm out of a full stepper field — and then the mask and the wafer are swept through it in opposite directions until the whole die has passed. When the field is done, the stage steps to the next one, exactly as a stepper does.

Nikon's own patent on the mechanism states the reason plainly: the point is to form a high-quality image of a large mask on a large wafer *even though the mask and wafer are larger than the area of optimum imaging properties* of the optics. The printed field length stops being a property of the glass. It becomes a property of how far the two stages can travel in synchrony, which is a mechanical problem, and mechanical problems have been more tractable than lens problems ever since.
sections.deeper_md: This is why the scan direction and the cross-scan direction are not symmetric in any modern tool, and why nearly every intra-field correction knob is described separately for the two axes. Cross-scan, you have whatever the slit width of the lens gives you and nothing else; along the scan, you have as much length as the stage will hold position over.

sections.heading: The speed ratio is the reduction ratio
sections.body_md:
Once you are scanning, the hard engineering moves from the optics to two stages that must stay locked together while moving fast. The mask and the wafer travel in opposite directions through the slit, and because the lens demagnifies, the wafer must move slower than the mask by exactly the demagnification factor. At 4× reduction that is a four-to-one speed ratio, and in a production tool of the mid-2000s it meant a wafer stage above 500 mm/s and a mask stage at 2.0 m/s, both floating on air bearings and driven by linear motors.

The tolerance on that lock is the number that should make you uncomfortable. Umatate and Matsuyama put the required on-wafer synchronisation accuracy at under 10 nm, while the two bodies are moving at a metre or more per second. Critical dimension control is where the error surfaces: a 60 nm feature is allowed about ±6 nm, and synchronisation error during the scan blurs the aerial image in the scan direction and eats straight into that budget.
sections.deeper_md: Synchronisation error is not reported as a single number but as two: the moving average of the position error over the slit transit, and the mean standard deviation around it. They do different damage. The moving average shifts where a feature lands, which reads out as overlay; the mean standard deviation smears the image while it is being integrated, which reads out as a loss of contrast and therefore of critical-dimension uniformity. A tool can be good at one and bad at the other, which is why both appear on the specification sheet.

sections.heading: Scanning averages the lens, and adds a new error
sections.body_md:
Here is the part that is genuinely counterintuitive, and it is the reason scanning is better than a big lens rather than merely cheaper. In a stepper, every point in the field is imaged by one fixed part of the lens, so whatever distortion that part has is printed faithfully, every time, at that point. In a scanner, a given point on the wafer is exposed continuously while it traverses the slit, so what it receives is the intensity-weighted average of the lens's distortion along the whole scan path.

Litel's patent work on intra-field distortion makes the decomposition explicit. The lens component depends only on the cross-scan coordinate and is repeatable; the scanning component depends only on position along the scan and carries both repeatable and non-repeatable parts. Averaging kills the lens's scan-direction distortion almost entirely — every row in the scan gets the same displacement — and replaces it with a term made entirely of stage dynamics. That is a good trade, because stage errors are measurable in real time and lens errors are not.
sections.deeper_md: The weighting function in that average is the slit's own intensity profile, which is why illuminator uniformity along the scan is a distortion specification and not merely a dose specification. A slit that is 2 percent brighter on one edge weights that part of the lens 2 percent more heavily in every field on every wafer, and the result appears as a systematic, repeatable intra-field signature that looks exactly like a lens error.

sections.heading: What it costs, and where the trade goes next
sections.body_md:
Throughput is what you pay with. A stepper's field time is one exposure; a scanner's is an acceleration, a constant-velocity scan long enough to cover the die, a deceleration, and a step — with the mask stage doing all of it at four times the distance. Modern tools attack that with brute acceleration: ASML quotes 8 g on the wafer stage and 32 g on the reticle stage of its High NA machines, against half and a quarter of that on the previous generation, to hold throughput above 185 wafers an hour.

The trade has now come back around. High-NA EUV buys resolution with a 0.55 numerical aperture and anamorphic optics that demagnify 4× in one direction and 8× in the other, and the price is an exposure field half the size of the previous generation's. Dies larger than that half-field have to be printed as two exposures and stitched. Which is the same problem the first scanner was invented to solve, arriving again from the other direction.
sections.deeper_md: Stitching is not simply two exposures side by side. The seam inherits the overlay error between the two fields, so features crossing it need design rules that keep critical structures away from the boundary, and any layer printed in one exposure has to register to a layer printed in two. The alternative — designing dies under the half-field limit and connecting them with advanced packaging — is the reason the reticle limit shows up in chiplet strategy discussions that appear to be about packaging.

glossary.definition: The patterned quartz plate holding the circuit image for one exposure field. At 4× reduction it carries features four times the printed size, which is why reticle defect specifications are looser than wafer ones by the same factor.
How much the projection optics demagnify, written 4× or 4:1. It sets both the mask-to-wafer feature scaling and, in a scanner, the ratio of reticle stage speed to wafer stage speed.
The area printed in one exposure before the stage steps. In a stepper it is bounded by the lens's well-corrected field; in a scanner only its width is, because its length is set by stage travel.

The narrow rectangle of illumination a scanner projects through the best-corrected band of the lens. Its width sets the cross-scan field; its intensity profile sets how the lens's distortion is weighted into the average.

glossary.term: Moving average and mean standard deviation (MA/MSD)
glossary.definition: The two statistics used to specify stage synchronisation during a scan. MA is the mean position error over a slit transit and appears as overlay; MSD is the spread about it and appears as image blur, so it costs contrast and CD uniformity.

Placement error as a function of position within one exposure field, as distinct from field-to-field error. In a scanner it decomposes into a repeatable lens term varying across the scan and a stage term varying along it.

Optics with different magnification along the two axes — 4× and 8× in High NA EUV — adopted because the larger mirrors needed for a 0.55 numerical aperture cannot pass the reflected beam at 4× in both directions without the beams clipping each other.

foundations.try_this: Do the synchronisation arithmetic for MNF's own stepper before the stage is finalised. Umatate and Matsuyama quote under 10 nm on-wafer synchronisation accuracy for a production scanner printing 60 nm features with a ±6 nm CD budget — a tenth of the feature. Apply the same tenth to a 2 µm printed feature and you get 200 nm, then ask what that means for the club's stage: what encoder resolution, what servo bandwidth, and at what sweep speed does the position error spectrum push past it? Then compare against the alternative the club already has, which is to step the DMD field and never scan at all, and write down which number decides it.
